questions.title: Confused about the definition of 'Hyperspherical Energy': Why is it defined as the inverse of distances rather than the sum of cosines?
questions.question_body: In Section 3.2, Equation (1), the paper defines Hyperspherical Energy (HE) as $\text{HE}(\bm{W}) := \sum_{i\neq j} \|\hat{\bm{w}}_i - \hat{\bm{w}}_j\|^{-1}$. Earlier in the abstract and introduction, it mentions HE captures 'pairwise neuron relationship' and 'uniformity'. Usually, measures of uniformity or repulsion involve maximizing distances or minimizing similarities (cosine similarity). Here, the formula sums the *inverse* of the Euclidean distance between normalized vectors. If two neurons are close together (distance $\to 0$), this term explodes to infinity. Is this formulation intended to act as a repulsive force where we want to *maximize* this energy to spread neurons out? Or is there a sign convention I am missing? The text says we want to 'preserve' this value, but doesn't explicitly state whether high or low energy corresponds to better semantic preservation in this specific context.

questions.title: Does Cayley parameterization restrict OFT from modeling reflections, and does this matter for image generation?
questions.question_body: Section 3.3 states that using Cayley parameterization ($\bm{R}=(\bm{I}+\bm{Q})(I-\bm{Q})^{-1}$) allows us to efficiently enforce orthogonality, but notes a limitation: it can only produce orthogonal matrices with determinant $1$ (special orthogonal group $SO(d)$), excluding reflections (determinant $-1$). The paper claims this limitation 'does not affect performance in practice.' However, mathematically, an orthogonal transformation includes both rotations and reflections. If a downstream task theoretically requires flipping the orientation of features (a reflection) to match the target distribution, OFT with Cayley parameterization might be fundamentally incapable of learning that specific transformation. Has anyone tested if allowing reflections actually helps in diffusion model finetuning, or is the feature space robust enough that rotations alone suffice?

questions.title: How does Re-scaled OFT preserve Hyperspherical Energy if magnitudes are changed?
questions.question_body: Section 3.4 introduces Re-scaled OFT with a diagonal matrix $\bm{D}$ containing learnable positive scalars $s_i$. The paper argues that 're-scaling neurons does not change the hyperspherical energy (the magnitude will be normalized out).' Looking at Eq (1), HE depends on $\hat{\bm{w}}_i = \bm{w}_i / \|\bm{w}_i\|$. If we update weights as $\bm{W}_{new} = \bm{R}\bm{W}^0\bm{D}$, then each column vector becomes scaled by its corresponding $s_i$. When we normalize these new columns to calculate HE, indeed the scalar factors cancel out ($s_i \bm{v} / \| s_i \bm{v} \| = \hat{\bm{v}}$). So strictly speaking, HE is preserved regardless of $s_i$. But if HE is purely angular and invariant to scale, why do we need to learn these scales at all? Doesn't this contradict the premise that preserving angles is sufficient? Or is the magnitude information critical for something else in diffusion models that isn't captured by HE?

questions.question_body:
Section 3.3 compares parameter efficiency between LoRA and OFT. For LoRA with rank $r'$, parameters are roughly $(d+n)r'$. For OFT with block size determined by $r$, parameters are roughly $d(d/r - 1)/2$. The paper simplifies this by assuming both ranks depend on dimension ($r=r'=\\alpha d$) leading to complexities of $O(d^2)$ vs $O(d)$. However, in practical implementations like Stable Diffusion's cross-attention layers, input dimension $d_{in}$ and output dimension $d_{out}$ are often different (e.g., projection layers). In LoRA, we usually have separate ranks for down-projection ($d_{out}\\times r'$) and up-projection ($r'\\times d_{in}$). In OFT's block diagonal approach described here, does $
olinebreak[4]\\mathbf R
olinebreak[4]$ operate on rows or columns? If it operates on rows (output dimension), how do we handle cases where input/output dims don't match perfectly for square block decomposition? Does the complexity analysis hold when applying OFT to non-square weight matrices found in Transformer attention heads?
